_comment: The one home for the rules this project states about how its own texts are written. Every language checker is generated from this file or reads it directly, so a rule's wording, its thresholds, its carve-outs, and its word lists are edited here and nowhere else; a checker that keeps its own copy of a list is drift to fold back. A path written as `~/...` resolves under the agent's own `.claude` directory, and every other path is relative to the repository root. `status` says whether a catcher runs the rule today: `held` means a catcher runs at a named harness event, in a gate, or at a named manual step; `stated-only` means no catcher runs it, which includes a script that exists and is armed nowhere; `claimed-but-absent` means a home names a catcher that does not carry the rule. Inside `catchers`, `partial` means the catcher reads part of the class or part of the surface. Inside `catchers.model`, `where` is a comma-separated list of homes, each one opening with the path of the checker that RUNS the law and naming the mechanism it runs through after `via`; `scripts/gen-language-consumers.py` keys each generated law body by that checker together with a surface, so a checker is handed the laws it actually holds and no others, and a home path under `~/` marks a law the reader's own personal layer owns and the package never ships. `armed` names the event or gate a catcher runs at; a catcher that runs at the PreToolUse event is recorded in `notes`, because the field's vocabulary holds no word for that event. Beside `rules` this file carries three sets the generator prints for a reader: `legend` defines the status words and the arming events, `surfaces` defines each surface with an example and states the block rule, and `question_index` maps a writer's question to the rules that answer it. A rule's `lists` field gives every set the rule names: an entry carrying `source` and `key` is READ out of that JSON file at build time, so the list can never drift; an entry carrying `home` and `members` was copied from a script that holds it in code, and the home is named so a reader knows a change there does not reach the page. To add a rule: append an entry with the next free id, a plain one-sentence `rule`, a `reader_test` a reader can apply to one sentence, the surfaces it binds, its `sources`, and `status` of `stated-only`; then wire or generate the catcher and record it under `catchers`. This file carries Russian pattern text as data, so `scripts/shipped-language-allowlist.json` owes it a `user_language_globs` entry before the shipped-language gate can pass.

rule_status.held: a catcher runs this rule today: at a named harness event, inside a gate, or at a named manual step
rule_status.stated-only: no catcher runs this rule, which includes a script that exists and is armed nowhere
rule_status.claimed-but-absent: some file names a catcher for this rule, and that catcher does not carry it

catcher_status.held: this catcher runs the class it names over the surface it names
catcher_status.partial: this catcher reads part of the class, or part of the surface
catcher_status.absent: no catcher of this kind runs the rule

armed.pre-commit: a gate refuses the commit until the text changes
armed.pre-push: a gate refuses the push until the text changes
armed.session-stop-hook: the session's reply is held at the end of the turn, and a correction is asked for before the text reaches the reader
armed.session-prompt-hook: the verdict on the previous reply is put in front of the session when the person sends their next message
armed.PreToolUse: the next tool call is denied, so the correction reaches the reader inside the same turn; a rule armed here records it in its notes, since the `armed` field's vocabulary holds no word for the event
armed.manual: a person runs the catcher over a file by hand, and nothing runs it on its own
armed.nowhere: no catcher runs the rule at any event

surfaces.note: A surface is a KIND of text, not a file, and one file carries several. The numbered requirements and acceptance criteria of a spec are spec-body; the Context paragraphs and User Story lines in that same file are human-prose. Two rules that would give opposite verdicts on one word therefore never meet on one sentence: they govern different blocks of the file. A text declares one primary surface, and a text published to someone outside the project carries `artifact` as well, with every rule binding either surface in force. Where two rules would still give opposite verdicts on one sentence, that is a defect in these rules: it is recorded and settled here, and a writer is never handed the choice.

A documentation page is human-prose, and it carries `artifact` as well once it is published outside the project.

model.law_text: no grading importance or quality without a concrete fact. Praising or grading the WORTH of a thing — a thought, a result, a phrase, a rhyme, a design, a change — with an evaluative word and no fact behind it is banned. Grading how important, how good, or how strong something is, up or down, is the reader's own act; the text states what the thing IS or DOES and lets the reader weigh it. Banned as a class in any language: «сильная мысль», «сильный результат», «красивая рифма», «в разы лучше», "a strong point", "a beautiful solution", "far better", used as a verdict on worth rather than a statement of fact. A word that carries a FACT stays: "cuts the query from 900ms to 40ms" is a fact and passes; "much faster" with no number is a grade and offends. The class covers both poles — inflating up and dramatizing down are one bias — and it grades ANY object, a result included.
